claims.text: Tungsten has important applications in fusion reactors but is limited by low-temperature, recrystallization, and irradiation-induced brittleness.
Laminated tungsten-based composites can improve both low- and high-temperature toughness of tungsten.
A conventional W/TiN/Ta composite has limited high-temperature ductility and toughness.
A micron-scale vanadium transition layer can be incorporated into a W/V/TiN/Ta laminated composite using spark plasma sintering.
Uniform spark-plasma-sintering conditions will make the control and V-containing composites comparable in microstructure apart from the V layer.
Mechanical testing from room temperature to 800 degrees Celsius or above simulates fusion-reactor service conditions.
Micron-scale V improves bonding at the W-TiN interface.
The V transition layer is coherent with the tungsten-side interface.
The V layer improves dislocation-slip transmission across the W-TiN interface.
The V layer reduces interfacial energy and creates a smoother transition between phases.
Reduced interfacial energy and a smoother phase transition lower the barrier to dislocation motion.
The V layer mitigates stress concentration at the W-TiN interface.
Improved dislocation transmission and reduced stress concentration delay crack initiation under high strain rates.
Delayed crack initiation increases high-temperature plastic strain and toughness.
W/V/TiN/Ta will exhibit a statistically significant increase in high-temperature plastic strain relative to W/TiN/Ta.
The V-containing composite is expected to show approximately a 17% increase in flexural strain.
The V-containing composite will have greater toughness, bending strength, and ductility than W/TiN/Ta.
A nanoscale Ni transition layer increased W/TiN/Ta flexural strength by 25.6% and flexural strain by 17.6%.
Micron-scale Ni, Ti, and V transition layers improve W-TiN interfacial joining and decrease the joining temperature.
The effect may depend on sintering temperature, V-layer thickness, and microstructural heterogeneity.
